speechtext: First, I would not say that they are not discharging their responsibility. There are many people down there who are saying "Thank God for the United Nations High Commission on Refugee". It is suggested that there are not enough security checks being done and that one RCMP officer is not enough down there. subsubtopic: ESTIMATED NUMBER OF SWINE FLU CASES
speechtext: Was a study conducted that would indicate the estimated number of swine flu cases that could occur in Canada before June 30, 1977 or any other date if no vaccination programme is instituted and, if not, what is the basis for supporting such a vaccination compaign?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ESTIMATED NUMBER OF SWINE FLU CASES
speechtext: Swine influenza is known to be related to the virus which caused the pandemic of 1918-19. In that pandemic, and estimated 40,000 Canadians died and there were approximately 20 million deaths worldwide. It has been learned from serological studies that less than two percent of the population under 50 years of age have antibodies to swine influenza, 60 per cent in the age group 50-64 years and 80 per cent in persons 65 years of age and over. If 40 per cent of those without antibody were to become infected in the first wave of a swine influenza epidemic, as happened last year with the A/Victoria epidemic, approximately 7.5 million Canadians would be involved. The proportion of these who would die or suffer severe illness compared with a milder form of the disease is unknown. If the severity of disease is similar to the Asian influenza epidemic of 1957, in which 5,000 Canadians died, preliminary studies have shown the benefit cost/ratio of the vaccination program to be approximately 11.1 dependent on an acceptance rate of 65 per cent in those eligible for vaccination.

The House resumed, from Friday, December 17, consideration in committee of Bill C-22, to amend the statute law relating to income tax-Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale)-Mr. Turner in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. When the committee rose on Friday, December 17, clause 1 of the bill was under consideration.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, you may recall that at four o'clock on Friday I believe I had completed my remarks. I will not take too much more of the time of the committee. I had indicated during the course of my remarks that the minister had said that those of us in this party who had spoken seemed to be arguing in favour of the abandonment of the RRSP principle. He went on to point out that there had to be something for the private sector, and in terms of the wage earner sector this was simply equality, or the RRSP was simply the equivalent device which would permit this section of the community to provide for retirement in a similar way. He pointed out that wage earners are allowed certain tax deductibility as a result of retirement plans developed in that area.
I hope I am not misinterpreting what the minister has said, but that is the way I interpreted one of his replies-that by arguing against RRSPs we were, in a sense, condemning all these of plans which are in operation on the part of wage earners. What we are saying is that if you examine the equivalent tax advantage to those who earn wages, as against the tax advantage to those in the private sector, and compare the incomes of the two groups, you will find that those in the wage area are receiving far less tax benefits than those who are in the professional and private areas who set their own tax plans under the RRSP system.
Imagine the dollar value to a man who is working in a mill and making $10,000 a year, in terms of the tax advantages he receives as a result of the deductions from his cheque as part of a retirement plan, as compared to the amount which is received by someone at the level of income in this House. There is no comparison whatsoever. That is why we still insist that the RRSP principle is taxation in reverse, the redistribution of income upward to the rich and away from those of average or below average income.
On the evidence before the minister's own eyes there is no valid argument against that proposition. If the minister wants to argue that the purpose of the tax system and of the RRSP, in terms of the distribution of wealth, is in line with the theory that it is appropriate that the greater tax advantage showed flow to higher income earners, I could accept that argument
Income Tax
and understand it as representing a philosophy behind this tax legislation.

Would the hon. member accept a question? Does he think that people who are self-employed or employed in companies without pension plans should be denied any tax exemptions for retirement purposes whatsoever?

Of course, that is not our position. What I am saying is that the tax advantage should be reduced on a scale which runs upward dependent upon the income, so as to be fair to both ends of the income scale. Under this proposal you are rewarding the higher income level and penalizing the lower income level. I do not believe this is a concept with which the hon. member who asked the question necessarily agrees. He has not quite grasped the concept yet. I see he is shaking his head. He has grasped the concept and I hope he agrees with it-that if you change the dollar amount of the deduction received as a result of the RRSP, and if you take the wage earner and give him a higher exemption in terms of what he is allowed to deduct, and work a progressive tax right through the legislation, I would, perhaps, find some reason to support this proposal. But on its present basis, the principle chosen awards the rich and penalizes the poor.

Does the hon. member believe that the same ceiling should be applied to the combined employer-employee contributions under pension plans? Does he not admit that under existing pension plans the combined employer-employee contribution sometimes exceeds the limit placed upon RRSPs?

Almost never, or very rarely. What we are talking about at the upper end has not really been a retirement plan at all, but a tax shelter, a tax dodge, a convenient way to put money in and out of a plan. You put it in at a high rate, and take a tax deduction, and withdraw at a low rate, denying the treasury $513 million every year, a very substantial sum. That is one tax dodge. There are all kinds of other tax dodges. The RHOP is to some extent a tax dodge as well. The principle of our opposition to clause 1 continues to be this: if you examine Carter's approach to taxation, you begin to introduce fairness in taxation, but as long as you build these anomalies which reward the rich and penalize the poor and those of average income in the tax system, you are doing nothing in terms of creating a tax system which embodies justness and fairness.
My hon. friend from Waterloo-Cambridge tells me the program also distorts the capital market. I think it does, by moving money into certain kinds of investment plans and away from other forms of savings such as Canada savings bonds which might be more desirable from a public point of view; other forms of public investment might be more desirable from the point of view of the economy as a whole.
I do not intend to take up the time of the committee much longer, but I do want it to understand that our opposition to clause 1 is not simply an attempt to deny the passage of this bill. We wish to give the government time to recognize what it

is doing, to take account of the effects upon society of a program which continues to redistribute income in reverse.

1 shook my head to the hon. gentleman. I have listened to him, and still I shake my head. He draws a comparison between the private sector and wage earners. It may be a matter of his personal definition, but it seems to me he should recognize that the vast number of people having the benefit of registered pension plans will themselves be in the private sector. It is true there are also many in the public sector; for example, employees of the government of Canada.
I am not sure how many days we have been debating this bill, but four or five days ago, on the first day of the debate on clause 1, the figures I put forward at that time indicated that the majority of those who are participating in RRSP are in receipt of incomes of $15,000 or less. So the hon. member's objection covers this particular group of people, one which obviously, from his viewpoint, does not consist of upper income people. It is fair, too, to point out that the percentage value of the RRSP deduction is greater for those at the lower end of the income scale than for those at the upper end of the scale, not in absolute terms but in terms of their income.
The hon. member shakes his head but that is a mathematical fact. What the hon. member is really saying is this: he feels that incomes should be equal throughout Canada, and if that is his theory the proposal he is making would be perfectly consistent with it. I would point out that we do have a progressive income tax rate and that a maximum is set under this program so that benefits do not go all the way up the income level: there is a ceiling. So if there is any rethinking to be done about the position which has been taken, I think it is the hon. member who should be doing the rethinking.
First, there are wage earners both in the private and public sector. Second, a majority of those having the benefit of RRSP are in receipt of incomes of $15,000 or less. Third, the percentage value of the deduction is greater for those at the lower income scale than for those further up in terms of their incomes. Finally, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, in advising that RRSP funds would, presumably, not be put in government investment. That is not true at all. Indeed, very many of them are held in the form of government of Canada and other government bonds.

I was advising the hon. member on something else. I was suggesting that the government is distorting the whole capital allocation system and in many ways forcing every other savings device to pay higher rates of interest in competition with the attractiveness of RRSP.
The minister has repeated what he said earlier, and I do not doubt the particular set of figures he is putting before the House. He said there are more people getting the benefit who make below $15,000 than people making over $15,000, and we accept that. We have asked the minister the dollar value of the total group below $15,000 in terms of the benefits they are

getting, in terms of the tax saving they are getting, and the subsequent loss to the treasury as against the total amount of dollars in the group above $15,000; and how does that work out on the basis of the number of individuals involved as against the tax savings for the individuals below $15,000 and the tax savings for those above $15,000?
When we asked the question a few days ago, the minister said he did not have that set of figures. That is the set of figures relative to the kind of argument we are making. What we are saying is that people in the higher income brackets are getting much more benefit because they can set aside larger sums of money than those in the lower tax brackets. I hope the minister has had a chance to review the request we have made for those figures regarding distribution and will be in a position to give them to the House.

The figures I cited to the hon. gentleman are those prepared from taxation statistics. I have to say that the particular orientation which the hon. gentleman seeks to support his argument has not been prepared by Revenue Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief comment with further reference to what the minister had to say. We are trying to make our point abundantly clear. The dollar limits that a person is allowed to take in terms of his retirement income are not fixed. The minister is right in saying that you can only go so far.
They are fixed.

I am agreeing with the minister. The thing the minister has not put his mind to, or does not want to put his mind to, is the value, to a person making $50,000 a year, of that particular deduction. It is something like 50 cents to a dollar that he is putting into the plan. If the guy is taxed at a 20 per cent tax rate or less, the value to him is in reverse; it is much less. That is why we say that this is income distribution in reverse. Can the minister answer that point?

In percentage terms, it is of greater value if you have an income of $10,000 and you can put $2,500 of it in RRSP or RPP, or even a lower amount. Obviously, you then have a greater percentage of your income going into the retirement plan than if your income is $25,000 and you are putting in $2,500. It is simple mathematics.
It is the value of the money to the individual.

The minister is saying, then, that it is good to have a low income because you then have a low tax rate. It is a terrible thing to be making a lot of money because then you have to pay tax at a higher rate. If those earning under $5,000 manage to have $5,000 in savings, then the minister's argument would be very apt. The point is that there is a relationship between the amount of money they make and the amount they can set aside in savings. It is only those with high incomes who can set aside larger sums of money. Then the argument is accurate that those with higher incomes, no matter which way
December 20, 1976

the minister wishes to explain it, get a much greater benefit out of these kinds of devices than those with lower incomes. I do not know of many guys working in the factory who can put aside $3,500 a year, let alone $5,500 a year. So it is really a spurious argument that is being made to suggest that those who are making less money are getting a greater benefit just because they have a lower marginal rate of tax.
In percentage terms, they are.

Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to enter this debate for three main reasons. The first is that it is of great interest to my constituents. There are many elderly people in my constituency, most of them of very modest means and very self-respecting people but without substantial income. Many of them own houses and they are finding things increasingly difficult, because of higher municipal taxes and higher cost of repairs, to keep their houses. Therefore, anything to do with pensions, particularly those pensions that are payable fairly soon, for this group of people who are getting older and need these pensions is of great interest to them.
The second reason for which I want to speak on this matter is that I think the very essence of the democratic socialist faith which I share with my colleagues, and which I think is a faith held fairly widely throughout the world, is equality, fairness and equity between individuals. There are some people, even those who write dictionaries and things like that, who see the essence of socialism in the proposals for public ownership. I, for one, think public ownership is a useful method, but it is not part of a sacred writ so far as I am concerned. It is only one method of dealing with things.
I think that most of what I learned about socialism came from R. H. Tawney, a famous English theologian, writer and economist, who wrote a book on the subject of Equality. I notice the minister is very kindly listening to me and I would recommend Equality to him as it is a very inspiring account of this basic philosophy.
The next point I want to make, the third reason why I am very anxious to speak on this subject, is that my own profession of law is based on the theory of equality. I share that profession with the minister and, indeed, the Prime Minister, for that matter. According to our English system, there were two bodies of law. There was the common law, and under the common law doctrine one of the basic rules was that everybody was entitled to equal justice before the courts. There was no discrimination, because you were well off or you were not well off. There was no discrimination between persons. The law, therefore, was based upon the principle of equality. But equality under the common law was not adequate, so it was extended through the doctrine of equity with which the minister is familiar. A whole new body of law came into being. One of the basic principles of the doctrine of equity which has been incorporated into our legal system is that equity is equality. That was one of the famous sayings that is constantly being referred to by the courts when they discuss the question of equity.
Income Tax
For these three reasons I was very anxious to speak on this subject. What I wanted to stress particularly has to do with the subject that has been raised a good deal in this debate, the so-called deferred income plans, the registered retirement savings plan and the registered pension plan. As I understand it, this legislation is changing, making more available and perhaps more attractive some of the provisions in regard to these matters. What I wanted to try to do was draw to the attention of the committee an excellent report by the National Council of Welfare on the personal income tax system in Canada. It is called "the hidden welfare system", and it deals with that which is paid to poor people by way of what we commonly know as welfare. However, it points out that while those payments have been made, another massive spending program continues virtually unnoticed. Like the highly visible welfare system for the poor, this program transfers money from government to individuals. In fact, it transfers far more money than the poor ever receive from their welfare system and its benefits go to millions of people.
By any reasonable definition of the term, it is a welfare program, except that it is not called a welfare program, and its principal beneficiaries, most assuredly, are not the poor. It is called the Income Tax Act, and I want to call to the attention of the minister once again-and I am sure he has had this called to his attention before-that we have in this country a welfare program which does not work for the poor, but under the various provisions of the Income Tax Act, in fact, works for those who are by no means poor and are by no means in serious need. I want to elaborate on that and refer again to the report I have mentioned. The report refers to various provisions of the Income Tax Act dealing with the collecting of taxes, as follows:
All the remaining sections of the Act constitute the hidden welfare system. In contrast to the first group of provisions (the collecting side of taxation), these sections bear no relation whatever to the tax system proper and would be unnecessary for its fair and efficient operation as a means of raising revenue. They were put in the act not because they are necessary for a technical measurement of income, but to give certain people a tax break-in other words, to provide financial assistance to certain groups and individuals.
These provisions take the form of deductions and exemptions from income, credits against tax, preferential tax rates, deferrals of tax and tax reductions. They are variously called tax incentives, tax preferences or loopholes.
Sometimes I think they are referred to, in a more general sense, as opportunities for tax shelter. The writer of this report says as follows:
A more accurate terminology, and the one we will use throughout this paper, would be to call them tax subsidies or tax expenditures. Taken together they define the spending side of taxation.
That these provisions are government subsidies is clearly demonstrated by an example. Let us consider someone who has an income of $20,000, $19,000 in wages and $1,000 in interest from a savings account. Under the existing tax provisions, a taxpayer is allowed to deduct up to $ 1,000 in interest to arrive at his taxable income; so he pays $380 less than the person whose total income is made up of wages. The subsidy is accomplished through an exemption from taxes. It never

appears as a government expenditure at all. Through these various savings schemes of special allowances and exemptions, a very large amount of money-I have seen the figure of $560 million-is paid out and, of course, there is no stigma attached to this. If a person is on welfare and gets a straight payment from the state when he needs it, there is certainly a stigma attached to that. However, on the other hand, if a person has a good tax lawyer and is able to maximize the benefits under the Income Tax Act, he is regarded as being rather clever, intelligent, up to date and shrewd. His efforts are applauded, generally speaking.
Those efforts are not only applauded, but they are encouraged by the form of the legislation we have. I, personally, do not have a great deal of admiration for astute lawyers or accountants who obtain tax subsidies for clients. I have a high opinion of the legal profession generally, being a member myself, but of all the shady parts of their activities, their work to get tax subsidies for those who do not need them is one of the shadiest. Just to give an example of the benefits-this point has been made before, but it is worth making again- this is a summary of the benefits under these various tax schemes:
-The temporary tax reduction provision cost Canadians $6.4 billion.
That is worked out as follows: if taxable income is under $5,000, the average benefit is $243.75. For a taxable income of between $5,000 and $10,000 the average benefit is $484.65. Then skipping some of the intermediate incomes, for an income of over $50,000 there is a tax benefit of $3,989.78. I find it difficult to imagine how in anything but a tax bill we could get away with giving a benefit of $3,989.78 to the wealthy and a benefit of $243.75 to those earning modest incomes.
How can we get away with that? The National Council of Welfare says this is unfair, wrong and not proceeding in a sensible manner. The amount is ten times higher for the well-to-do. This is something which has to be changed if we are to make reality of phrases like the "just society". I know most people do not like reading about income tax. I am not a particulary enthusiastic reader on the subject myself. People do not care to read about it, but when we look at the whole picture and find the hidden tax exemptions, we begin to understand that a gross injustice is being perpetrated throughout our tax system.
I wish to proceed and deal specifically with registered retirement savings plans. As is well known, each taxpayer is allowed to put a certain portion of his income into a registered retirement savings plan, and that amount is totally exempt from taxation. There are, of course, limits, and I understand that one of the purposes of this bill is to extend or expand the limits to some extent. However, these deferred income plans do not work equally for the poor as they do for the well-to-do. With regard to benefits, the provision cost Canadians in 1974 an estimated $515 million. About half a billion dollars went in benefits primarily to those with high incomes.
Let me illustrate that. The average tax saving for those earning under $5,000 is $1.02, or .5 per cent of all tax savings.

Those earning from $5,000 to $10,000 save $9.81, or 7 per cent of all tax savings. Those earning between $5,000 to $10,000 save $9.81, or 7 per cent of all tax savings. Those earning between $10,000 and $15,000 have an average tax saving of $38.43. Those earning $15,000 to $20,000 save $125.01. Those earning over $20,000 have a tax saving of $551.88, or 57.3 per cent of all the benefits. That percentage is for people earning over $20,000, people who surely do not need special subsidies to enable them to save money for their old age. If the latter percentage is added to the savings of those earning between $15,000 and $20,000, the total tax benefit is 76 per cent of all tax savings. I think the effect of the present legislation will increase the benefit for this particular group of high income people.
I want to deal with another aspect of the subject, and then I will be through. I want to deal with the question of the option in connection with the savings plan given to people at age 71. In this respect I am getting my information from a brief submitted to the minister by the National Association of Canadian Credit Unions which deals with section 146 of the act and the registered retirement savings plan.
According to the bill, at age 71 you have two choices: you may use all, or a portion, of the funds to purchase a life annuity, or you may receive, all or a portion, of the funds in taxable income. If you receive it all in taxable income at one time, a very substantial amount of it is taxed away-so that is not a very satisfactory option. If you take the other option you are forced to go to a life annuity-you are forced to take out an insurance policy. It is a rigid, inflexible and unsatisfactory choice, and something has to be done about it. It certainly does not suit the elderly people in my riding to be told, when they reach the age of 71, that they have to take all their savings at once and be taxed on it for one year or, alternatively, that they have to buy a life annuity-not a term annuity, but an obligatory life annuity.
As I understand it-and if I am wrong I am sure the minister will correct me-this was well put in a brief submitted by the Consumers' Association of Canada which said that life annuities are very profitable-but for their issuers, not the buyers. I see no need for this bonus to assist or aid the life insurance companies to sell their annuities if they are having any difficulty selling.
To conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I feel obliged to oppose this bill because it seems to me to perpetuate an unjust system, a hidden welfare system; it seems, to me, contrary to the principles I believe in and, lastly, I believe it is quite contrary to the interests of my constituents.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Greenwood, as he always does, has clarified the discussion considerably by restating the arguments that have been put forward. I should like to deal with them briefly. He lays considerable emphasis on the quality of equity as being important. Perhaps the best thing I can do is refer him to my remarks at page 1626 of Hansard where I pointed out that it

December 20,1976

was specifically because of the concern about equity as between recipients of retirement pension and registered retirement savings plans that the annuity requirement was inserted in the first place. To have done otherwise would have been to give to the person the hon. member for New Westminster was talking about, the self-employed person, a benefit which the recipient, a union member of an employee pension plan, would not have been able to have. Perhaps 1 could refer him to that because it was in the interests of equity that the provision was put in.
With regard to the question of householders, I must say that I know the hon. member's riding and I have people in similar situations in my own riding. I have to say quite clearly that this provision is not of any assistance to retired people. It does not pretend to be, because there are other provisions in the Income Tax Act such as the exemption for people over 65 which in the year 1976 amounts to $1,307 and the $1,000 exemption for either interest or pension income which are obviously directed to the group the hon. member referred to. I think that group would agree, if we put the question to them, that they would support measures in the Income Tax Act which will enable their children to set adequate sums aside to provide for their retirement income. That is the purpose of the RRSP as, indeed, is the case with deductions for registered pension plans.
On the question of equity or equality on which the hon. member laid some stress, he really clarified the debate here. What he is talking about is equality in terms of tax money saved. What we are talking about is equality in terms of up to a certain limit-a percentage of income against which the registered retirement savings plan deductions can be taken. I suppose the real question one would have to put to them is this: Given three incomes-$7,500, $10,000 or $15,000, what is the equal amount that it would be reasonable to save throughout the whole community in relation to pension incomes? We have said: Up to a certain point, equality in percentage terms; then it drops off as the income goes up. I think the suggestion on the other side is that there should be a fixed amount of tax benefit available for people saving for retirement income. That is a different concept and it is not one I happen to agree with because it seems to me there is fairness in it up to a certain point and then, of course, it falls off again.
The hon. member set out some figures with regard to the value of these deductions on particular incomes. I am not going to accept or deny their accuracy. They illustrate that the higher you go in the income scale, the larger absolute amount of tax-the larger percentage amount of income you pay in tax. In that case, quite naturally, a deduction like this is going to save them more tax than those on lower incomes. The hon. member's figures illustrate the fact that the income tax system is structured to lighten the load at the lower end and make it progressively heavier as it goes up.
It seems to me the crux of the debate is as between equality in actual dollar amounts or percentage equality up to a certain point when that falls off as income goes up. I go back to the point I made to the hon. member for New Westminster: in
Income Tax
percentage terms, this represents a greater value at the lower end of the income scale. In absolute dollars it does not. On the other hand, the tax burden at the upper end of the income scale is heavier.

Mr. Chairman, I want to put two questions to the minister. He compared his constituency with mine, and I agree they are similar. He suggested that I have been referring to retired people. I appreciate that retired people are not included in this, but there are a lot of people in both our constituencies, in their sixties, not yet retired but who will retire soon. They do not get the full benefit of this. On the other point, he says the provision provides for equality of opportunity. I say there should be actual equality in fixed deductions.
In actual dollar terms?
That is exactly what I am saying. I should like to suggest to the minister that that is precisely what we need if we are to have a fair system generally.

The hon. member is saying that as the majority of contributors have an income of under $15,000, we would have to decide at what limit we set the maximum tax benefit. Should it be $7,500? It seems to me, in our system, which is on a percentage basis, that should be subject to a certain maximum and the percentage is better. At least the hon. member has made his party's position clear.

Mr. Chairman, at page 2110 of Hansard for last Friday there was an exchange between the minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should like to put some questions to the minister arising from that exchange. From my reading of the proceedings of that day touching on clause 1 of the bill, I see that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made it a particular point to comment on the government's pension plan and employee superannuation plans. As reported at the top of page 2110 of Hansard, the minister said:
I suppose the most difficult question hon. members have had to deal with in this pension debate has been the question of the indexing of public service pensions. I am inclined to say to the critics that it seems to me that their objections fail to come to terms with a rather more fundamental issue in our community; that rather than taking away the opportunity to keep the pension in real terms to wherever the economy takes it, we should be concerned about the fact that many private plans do not have this, so that private plans being sold now will not yield in real terms what the participant is expecting. This is a matter of real concern.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, as reported at the top of page 2111 of Hansard:
-that if there is a difference between public plans and private plans, the thing to do is not to take escalation away from the public plan but to build escalation into the private plans.
My first question to the minister is this: Is the minister suggesting that somehow private plans which are now in existence or will come into existence should be indexed to take into account whatever inflationary forces the government may

December 20, 1976
Income Tax
permit in the economy? If so, how does he envisage private pension plans being funded if there is that type of indexing?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman did not quote my rejoinder, printed on page 2111, namely: "If it can be done." As I have told the House previously on a number of occasions, one of the purposes of the retirement income study is to see to what extent we can contrive to protect the people who are making private arrangements with benefits comparable to those in the public sector. It may not be possible to do that; but I am suggesting that unless this is done, over time there will be a very substantial pressure on whatever government happens to be in power for converting the retirement arrangements to public pensions.

Will the minister indicate if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was correct in stating, as reported on page 2111, that if there is a difference between public plans and private plans, "the thing to do is not to take escalation away from the public plan but to build escalation into the private plans?" I am not talking about any supplementary plan which may be applied in conjunction with the private plan. The hon. member's wording is clear. He was talking about an escalation in the private plan itself. I see the minister laughs. Perhaps he can tell the committee what he finds so funny.
That is exactly the point. I said that if that can be done it would be very desirable to keep the pensions of private pension recipients stable in real terms.

Mr. Chairman, that brings me back to my initial question. Can the minister suggest how a private plan could actually fund such an indexed program? Private plans do not have the access to tax revenue which is available to the federal government. They do not have the right to change plans. The federal government may find in future that it must change its plan in order to skate itself "on-side". In short, why would the minister even imply that private plans may somehow fund indexed pensions in future, unless he has some hard facts or some suggestion to make to show how this can be done in the private sector?
Mr. Chairman, I have repeatedly said in this debate, as I said a moment ago, that is a purpose of the retirement income study.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member reply to the suggestion raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, namely, that it would be preferable to shift private pension plans more into the public sector? I notice that the minister commented about there being worth-while investment funds in private sector plans and that he would sooner see them left in the private sector. Actually, I am asking for an assurance rather than raising a question. I want the minister to assure us that there will be no move on the part of his ministry or the present administration which will somehow alter the position of private pension plans in the general pension structure of this country in favour of more public plans.

Mr. Chairman, may I read what I said, as reported on page 2110 of Hansard:
My preference would be to leave a maximum amount of enterprise in private hands.

Mr. Chairman, that answer alarms me. The minister suggested that it would be his preference. Can he not give an assurance now that the government does not further intend to shift pensions in the private sector to the public sector?
Mr. Chairman, I would have to await the outcome of the retirement income study, but my preference is to leave it in private hands. I think that is what I said previously.

Mr. Chairman, many hon. members asked the minister if it is possible to have funds in an RRSP placed, on retirement, in a separate trust for the benefit of the plan holder. They would be placing such funds in a trust instead of an annuity. Some plan holders might find the annuity provision less advantageous than the privilege of being allowed to handle their funds independently and placing them in a separate trust. If I understood correctly, the minister said that the government would review such situation or that the committee reviewing the private incomes would look at the matter.
May I ask the minister if it is correct that several months ago Revenue Canada provided Canadians with what was called a third alternative, an amended registered retirement savings plans which Revenue Canada indicated was within the purview of the act. In short, they proposed that the capital in the amended plan would remain in the hands of a trustee, to be distributed at death to the beneficiaries of the plan holder if there was a residual amount. In the meantime, no annuity would be required, according to Revenue Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am advised that there is no provision in the law for this. I would have to check the accuracy of the hon. gentleman's suggestion, namely, one that Revenue Canada have been offering the proposal the hon. gentleman has described.

Mr. Chairman, may I direct the minister's attention to a column written by Diane Cohen, an expert in whom the minister takes great stock. I have often heard him extolling her virtues. The column which I shall quote in part appeared in the Calgary Herald on May 21, 1976, and says exactly what I have just said, namely, that such a trust could be established within the act. Miss Cohen then went on to say:
When news of this third alternative became known across the country, trust and insurance companies, as well as federal tax bureaux were inundated with requests for further details. Trust and insurance companies knew nothing about it. Revenue Canada reaffirmed its new interpretation of the Income Tax Act-
She went on to say:
But. . . the Department of Finance, which writes income tax law, disapproved of the new interpretation. It was not, they said, their intention to favour self-employed people who could put more money into RRSPs than wage and salary earners. Why, they said, should a self-employed person be able to control his/her own investments, when a salaried person who contributed to a company pension had no control over his/her investment?
December 20, 1976

Revenue Canada responded that while the Department of Finance may write the law, it is within the purview of Revenue Canada to interpret it. Revenue Canada said its interpretation ... the third alternative... stood. Finance countered that if Revenue Canada persisted, Finance would rewrite the law.
I ask, is what Miss Cohen related in that column substantially true? Was there a kind of feud going on with Revenue Canada interpreting the Income Tax Act one way, and Finance saying they did not agree, and if they persisted in their approach, they would have to rewrite the law?
Mr. Chairman, considering the hon. member's source, I would have to say probably it is not true.

We have been assured by certain members to our left that this debate may go on for a considerable time. If it does, will the minister consult with his staff to find out whether this type of interpretation was put forth by Revenue Canada? This is quite important. The minister has repeatedly stated that this is under study. If, in fact, the Department of Finance are so adamantly opposed that they have even suggested to Revenue Canada they would amend the law to ensure that it would not be done, before the committee on the whole stage ends the minister should be asked at least to check with his staff to find out whether there was this type of debate between Revenue Canada's interpretation of what could be done under the Income Tax Act and whether they in fact stated that if Revenue Canada persisted in that interpretation, they would have to rewrite the law.
Mr. Chairman, I am advised it was not a battle, but under clause 56 any possibility of such an interpretation will be headed off.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to take a few minutes to make the central point we have been making in the debate to the government, namely, that we do not feel we have an equitable tax system in this country. The minister stated in the debate that the percentage savings in pension plans, and so on, are greater or can be greater for those at the low income end of the scale than for those at the high income end. I agree with him. However, we in this party are interested in equating equality of condition. That is the most important thing we have to do. The bill before us has good in it.
Some clauses will help widen the gap between the rich and the poor, as has been argued by many members of this party during the past few days.
The Minister of Finance has been playing Santa Claus with some of the wealthier people. It is a Christmas bonus he is giving to some wealthier people just before Christmas. This is being done in three or four places in the bill before us. It is that type of Christmas bonus I am in no hurry to expedite. We do not need to give any more gifts to the wealthier people of this country. This was recently summed up in a report by the National Council of Welfare on the personal income tax system in Canada. We heard about this in November, 1975. I quote from page 1 of the report:
Income Tax
There are two welfare systems in Canada-one for the poor, the other for everyone else.
Of the welfare system for the poor, little need be said. It is well known to every Canadian. The high visibility of social assistance and other income security programs keeps them continually in the public view. The fear that these programs are being rampantly abused, in spite of all the evidence to the contrary, is constantly invoked. The question of whether government can afford this expenditure, regardless of the number of families who must rely on these programs as their only source of income, is passionately debated.
Later in the report they talk about the other welfare system in this country, namely, all the tax loopholes that are available to many Canadians. Of course, the tax loopholes are widened in this bill. It gives a few extra benefits to primarily the middle and upper income people in this country.
In their report they give some statistics to back up what they are saying in their assertion that there is a hidden welfare system. I quote:
Only 17 out of approximately 60 subsidies in the Income Tax Act are included in that $6.4 billion.
They are talking about $6.4 billion that was in effect lost to the treasury in 1974 because of the various income tax clauses and the various benefits available to the people of Canada. They point out that for the most part these give-aways and exemptions are primarily for the upper and middle income groups. On page 17 of the report there is an interesting table. It should be studied by all members of this House who are interested in creating equality of condition in this country. The table points out that for those earning under $5,000, the average benefit from the taxation system, including all the various benefits and deductions, is $243 a year. For those earning between $15,000 and $20,000, the average benefit is $1,177. That is significantly more than the guy earning $5,000. For those earning over $50,000, the average benefit is $3,989.
I am not complaining about this. I am saying that the dollar value being paid out by the government goes much more sharply to those in the middle and upper income brackets. One of the ironies of the situation is that people do not complain about this type of welfare or transfer payment to individuals if it is through the taxation system. However, they do complain if it comes from the government in the form of a welfare cheque, unemployment insurance cheque or something of that sort. I do not think that is right. At page 18 of the report the council talks about benefits going to the wealthy of this country. They show a chart with the percentage in total benefits from the various tax subsidies. They analyse 17 tax subsidies in our tax system. They first look at those who earn under $5,000 annually.
The percentage of all tax filers who made under $5,000 in 1974 is higher than most of us in this chamber think. It was 38.4 per cent of all Canadians. Well over one-third of all Canadians earned less than $5,000 that year. The percentage in total benefits under this system, drafted by the Government of the "just society", was 12.5 per cent. If you earned between $5,000 and $10,000 a year two years ago, you were in a group with 31.5 per cent of the Canadian people and received 27.9 per cent of the total benefits available under our income tax

December 20, 1976
Income Tax
system. You were slightly better off if you were in that tax group. However, you were still being cheated or were losing out with regard to receiving your fair value of the tax benefits available under the laws drafted by this parliament.
If you earned between $10,000 and $15,000-a decent middle income two or three years ago-you were in a group along with 18.7 per cent of the Canadian people. That group received 26.5 per cent of the taxation benefits. It will be seen that once you get a middle income figure, you start to receive more than your fair share of the taxation benefits available under the law drafted by this government which believes in equality and justice. If you earned slightly over the middle income salary in 1974, between $15,000 and $20,000, you were among 6.8 per cent of the population. That group received 14.3 per cent of the benefits of the taxation system. In other words, the ratio is almost two to one in favour of the upper middle income Canadian. If a person makes over $20,000, which is the final figure in the table, he is a member of a very select group because only 4.6 per cent of Canadians make over $20,000. Yet this same small select group receives 18.8 per cent of the tax benefits.
This type of table and the table that I referred to briefly a few moments ago essentially summarizes the point that we in this party are making, namely, that the tax system of this country, in terms of real dollars and equality of condition, is a very unfair one. It is, therefore, incumbent upon us as parliamentarians to make sure that we make this point as often as possible to the minister and his officials. We are not satisfied with a taxation system that discriminates in terms of constant dollars against the poor or those of low income, or even those taxpayers of middle income.
The bill before the committee today, Mr. Chairman, is going to widen the gap in three or four respects. This is why, in essence, it is a bill that the government wants to rush through before Christmas. It contains a Christmas bonus for a number of the more wealthy Canadians. It is a Santa Claus bill containing a Christmas bonus for some of our wealthy Canadians. Let me list what these bonuses are. I am sure Conservative members are interested in the first one, which is the famous surtax on incomes which was implemented during the inflation debate a year ago in this chamber. A 10 per cent surtax was placed on incomes of individual taxpayers in Canada who paid more than $8,000 a year income tax. This provision is to end at the end of this year, but I do not see why it should end. As I say, this provision will be a Christmas bonus for the more wealthy people of this country. Very few people in this country, certainly in my area, pay more than $8,000 a year in income tax; those who do do not need this kind of bonus. The money should be spent on helping the poor, on stimulating the economy, on reducing inequities and providing jobs for the people of this country.
This provision means that a person paying $8,100 income tax would have had to pay an extra $ 10. He will now save this extra $10. A person paying $9,000 income tax will save $100

once this bill goes through. This is the kind of gift I am not that anxious to give the wealthy people of this country. It is a Christmas gift of $100 by the government of Canada.
The second bonus has already been referred to today by my colleagues, namely, the deferred income plan. We are increasing the limit on the amount we may contribute to a registered retirement savings plan or a registered pension plan. The minister says that the average wage is around $15,000 or less, but as my colleague for Waterloo-Cambridge has said, we would like to see some statistics in terms of constant dollars. My guess is that people in the upper half of the income scale get a lot more in terms of tax savings and benefits down the road from registered retirement savings plans than do those in the bottom half of the income scale. If we raise the limit even more, we are providing even bigger tax shelters, tax give-aways or tax breaks to those already making a lot of money.
I know that the minister argues that if a person makes $10,000 and receives tax benefits amounting to $5,000, he is getting a tax shelter for one-half of his income, whereas if a person makes $50,000 a year and he receives back $5,000 he is only getting a tax shelter for 10 per cent of his income. But the minister knows it does not work that way. If you are making $10,000 or less in this country, you do not save a very large proportion of your income through a tax shelter plan; you have a progressive taxation rate. You are really dealing with a 50-cent dollar or an 80-cent dollar, which again works against the interests of the low-paid people of this country.
This bill seeks to raise the amount that can be contributed to a retirement pension plan from $2,500 a year to $3,500 a year. I maintain that if you look down the road a few years you will find that the overwhelming good received by Canadians from this will fall primarily into the pockets of the wealthy Canadians in this country. The same is true of registered retirement savings plans; the limits are being raised from $4,000 a year to $5,500 a year for people with no employer pension plan, and for those with a plan from $2,500 to $3,500 a year. Again I suggest that the benefits that flow from this in the main go to people in the upper income brackets.
Then we have the deferred profit-sharing plans. The ceiling on the amount employers may contribute is being raised from $2,500 to $3,500. This kind of plan helps the wealthier 5 per cent, 10 per cent, 15 per cent or 20 per cent of the Canadian population, rather than the lowest paid 5 per cent, 10 per cent, 15 per cent or even 50 or 60 per cent of the Canadian population.
In his budget papers on May 25, I believe it was, the minister said that all the changes regarding RRSPs, and so on, would effect about 300,000 people who were presently contributing to these plans. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, a lot of the money the Canadian government is giving away in terms of tax shelters for high income people which have been developed over the years should be redirected to those of low income; the money should be shifted away to those who really need it so they are given a financial break and the economy is stimulated. Rather than create tax shelters for the wealthy and middle income people in this country, we should put more
December 20,1976

money into improving pension plans, something the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been advocating for years in this House, be it improvement of old age pensions, widows' pensions or war veterans' pensions. If this were done, I maintain this would be a much better country to live in.
However, Mr. Chairman, I realize that my priorities are different from those of the government across the way. I believe in an egalitarian society. I believe in equality of condition. I believe that those who are wealthy in this country must be willing to sacrifice a great deal in order to help those at the bottom of the income ladder. Under this government the very reverse of this has been happening; the gap has been growing since 1968, instead of diminishing. I can quote table after table to prove that. We should create more jobs so the poor can make a contribution to society, rather than provide more jobs for lawyers and accountants to figure out how their wealthy clients can take advantage of various tax shelters that have been built into this system by this and previous ministers to the tune of $6.4 billion, according to the welfare report of 1974.

I have just a few points, Mr. Chairman. First of all, I am glad that the surtax on incomes has been taken off, since I think it is retrogressive in many ways. In levying income tax we tend to forget what the take-home pay is, which is the important thing to a worker. If income tax is too high, wages become too high since each group in society attempts to justify what it receives-in other words, what a person takes home. This tendency has been accentuated by the surtax.
In the province of Manitoba, with an NDP government, those with taxable incomes in excess of $30,000 are taxed at the rate of 70 per cent. Not only is this heavy tax detrimental to working, but it promotes operations outside the tax system. As a result, there are many operations of a commercial nature that take place outside the tax system and are therefore not subject to the tax. There are many examples of this.
Let me bring to the attention of the minister a matter on which I have received representations. I think it is an important matter in that we all want to promote small business. Many small businessmen are active in the contracting business, and one such area relates to the operation of earth-moving machinery. Let me refer to the regulations and schedule D regarding heavy equipment. The allowable depreciation has been drastically reduced from 50 per cent to 30 per cent. According to my information, this change resulted in a television program on "W-5" which indicated this was a tax shelter for certain people. My accountants have indicated to me that this is in fact the case.
When the government moved to reduce this summarily from 50 per cent to 30 per cent, it put a lot of small operators out of business. The suggestion is that the minister should try to restore the 50 per cent depreciation and find some regulation that would do away with those opportunities for people to use this as a tax shelter. Perhaps it should be confined to those
Income Tax
individuals who have a bona fide record of bidding for these jobs.
It is my understanding that these earth-moving machines cost from $50,000 to $100,000. Most contractors prefer contract bidding as it encourages individuals to get into the business with one machine, perhaps as a one-man operation. This particular regulation puts these one-man operations at a disadvantage in comparison to the larger firms which have many machines and a much better access to financing. The regulation, as I understand it, has had the effect of preventing many individuals from entering this contracting business. They might buy one machine and gradually expand, but they find it difficult to finance $75,000 or $100,000, particularly when they are only allowed to depreciate to the extent of 30 per cent in the first year. Perhaps if this could be returned to 50 per cent it would make it more easy for the small operators to get into this heavy-equipment contracting business.
Perhaps the minister might care to reply.

Mr. Chairman, I can advise the hon. member that following an order in council of December 2, the 50 per cent rate was restored in respect of power earth-moving equipment, class 22, and this will be published in the Canada Gazette for December 22, 1976.

I am sure this will be received with enthusiasm by these individuals. Let me turn now to the proposal regarding cattle that must be destroyed by government order. As a result of representations, I understand this is a contentious matter. The amendment will, in effect, allow a farmer to spread his income as a result of the destruction of his cattle over two years. If this is the case I should like to ask the minister if it has received the approval of cattlemen. I think there are certain weaknesses in relation to the two-year period, and I would appreciate an explanation from the minister.
Mr. Chairman, this comes under clause 30, and I wonder if we might postpone it until that time.
I would be glad to hear from the minister then, Mr. Chairman. If this measure is not passed by the end of the year, will there be any lapsing provisions and, if so, what are they?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, it seems it will not be a merry Christmas for some of the poor people, if we pass this bill. I understand some hon. members would like to see it passed as soon as possible as it will be of great advantage to a certain segment of the population. It amuses me to note that apparently it is only in ridings represented by the NDP that we have minimum and low-wage earners. This is rather surprising when we consider the fact that 38.4 per cent of the workers in

December 20, 1976
Income Tax
this country earn less than $5,000 per year. That fact seems to have escaped the attention of a number of members in other parties. I presume they are not very familiar with the incomes of a number of people in their areas.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said the other day that in his opinion there was equality under the Income Tax Act and that there was no inequality developing in the general population. It seems to me that is not true, and should be obvious to almost everyone. It may not be obvious to a lot of members of parliament who do not get much time to talk to the general population, but it should be a fact readily discernible in the various municipalities and from the increasing number of people on welfare. It should be obvious from a consideration of income tax brackets and the number of people living on minimum wages below the poverty line. I do not expect the parliamentary secretary to realize this from his lofty position. Perhaps it is time that we had another look at the situation.
It was very interesting to me when I considered the number of clauses in this bill and then looked at the hidden welfare system referred to by the National Council on Welfare. Perhaps this organization is directed toward welfare. When you read the list, you see mentioned tenants' associations, poverty groups, and low income groups-so probably it is slanted in that direction. There are a number of inequities in the act, and every member of parliament knows it. I am sure that many members of parliament, just as private industry across this country, have hired tax experts to look for the tax loopholes in order to get the greatest tax benefit. That is highly commendable; but in many cases it is cheating. They know it, and everybody else knows it. It may not be cheating from the moral standpoint of some people, but from my own it is.
I, as a member of parliament, paid $6,816 last year on a gross income of $27,000, with a taxable income of $21,000. It would not have been difficult for me to have reduced that figure by $2,000 or $3,000. I own farm property, and all I need to do is list the farm property and write off some of that money. I have never done so, because I consider it would be dishonest. I do not believe many members of the House feel that way, or we would look at some of the deductions we allow.
I am not thinking about the exotic tax havens used by some people. I am talking about the whole of the tax structure. I am talking about the loopholes in the general taxation laws which allow for great expenditure out of the tax dollar of those able to afford it. Seventeen of these examples out of approximately 60 subsidies to the wealthy produce approximately $6.4 billion. The National Council of Welfare, referring to personal income tax, considers this to be the spending side of income tax. If the government does not raise this money by exemptions, then obviously they are spending the money. Because they have collected it, it must be available for the general population.
What would $6.5 billion provide? I presume that if we had a sum as large as this to spend, we would be able to provide everyone in the country with an income above the poverty

level. That might be worth-while, because I find that poverty begets poverty. Those who are living below the poverty line are not able to raise themselves above that level. Family after family falls into this category. We have kept the native population in that category for years and years, and even with considerable government assistance it has been impossible for many of them to raise their standards to the point at which they can see an end to poverty. We hand them a few bucks, as we have done in connection with the James Bay project, and say this should satisfy them for a little while. It may satisfy one generation, but the money will go and they will not get out of the poverty syndrome; they will not get out of it until they have money to spend like other Canadians.
If we allow the rich to write off income tax, we are giving them a subsidy, we are making an expenditure of $6.5 billion in their direction, and we are not making that kind of expenditure upon the poor to make sure they are no longer poor! That is the wish of the people I represent and I am sure it is the wish of the majority of people in every riding who have an opportunity to know what we are doing with our expenditure from income tax. In the United States the government must explain not only the expenditure they make but the expenditure they allow in deductions through the tax structure. Both items are presented and must be justified.
One of the insidious things about the deductions allowed for income tax is that many of them were considered to be expediencies on only one occasion and then they continued indefinitely in the tax structure, known only to tax experts and to those who are out to tell people how they could save considerable sums of money beyond the expense of such professional advice. We now have an opportunity to look at many of these taxes and to read the information which the Welfare Council has provided. That information is very damaging to the whole of the income tax structure and to the idea of a progressive income tax.
Everyone in this country believes in progressive taxation. I am sure the minister does. I am sure I do. The difference is, the minister knows we do not have a progressive tax structure, and I do not know this. I am still foolish enough to think that if we pay the rich by providing demogrants, we should get the money back. But that is not true. If we pay the old age pension to a millionaire who does not need it, we do not get the money back. There is no reason why we should not get that money back. As the former member for Temascamingue said in the House so many times, there is no reason we cannot pay, as a demogrant, a guaranteed annual income of a reasonable amount to everyone and take it back if it is not needed under the income tax structure. But we cannot do this because there are so many loopholes available to those in the higher brackets but not to those at the bottom level.
Let me give one example. We are going to allow the saving of some money to buy a house and then we say it is necessary, first of all, for people to save $1,000. I do not know of many young people in this country who have never owned a house, who are making $10,000, who are renting an apartment, paying for furniture, paying for their car, paying for a young
December 20, 1976

family they may have acquired, and making the other expenditures they have to make as newlyweds and who are fortunate enough to be able to save SI,000. Of course, no difficulty is encountered by persons in the higher income brackets who have lived in a luxurious apartment for a long time: they can get this tax benefit. If hon. members look at the figures, they will find there are many more people taking advantage of this concession in the high level brackets than in the low level brackets. There are a couple of tax experts sitting on the floor of the House advising the minister. Both of them are young people. But I will bet they never advise the minister in terms of what their needs are. They advise him in terms of what the act provides and what the government wishes to accomplish in that respect. I am sure there is very seldom any practical application when it comes to changing the income tax structure. If you were to raise the personal exemption of the poor people by $100, they would be very grateful. It would not amount to very much, but they would be very grateful.
If you give that same benefit to those in the high income bracket, they would not be very grateful; they would want considerably more and they would get more even out of $ 100. The benefit to them would be considerably larger than it would be to those on lower incomes.
I have heard of a large corporation in this country, a multinational corporation which is worth probably $1 billion. 1 understand that in 1974 they paid $8,000 in income tax. You and I may have come close to paying that ourselves, and yet we are certainly not in their class, but the tax structure in this country is such that all the time we are giving a hand-out to those who do not need it. In the case of income tax, we take it out of the hands of those who need the money, because if you can save $61/2 billion out of the income tax structure it comes from those who most need benefits from the government. The only reason we collect taxes is to help pay the expenditures of the country. If there is any other reason for collecting money, I fail to see it because this government has not done very much to establish corporations, industries or Crown corporations for the benefit of the ordinary Canadian. In fact, many of the directions in which they have gone have been contrary to the wishes of the general population. That includes CDC in which I, for one, had very high hopes, it being the kind of corporation, I thought, that might work for the average Canadian.
The benefits that the Canadian population will get from the Canadian government will come out of taxes, the great bulk of which is raised from corporation taxes. Therefore, if you use the tax structure to help the rich, this will be done at the expense and to the detriment of the poor. In my opinion, that income tax structure would be a much better one if no deductions of any kind were made, which would mean that you could keep the rate of tax very low. You could set a floor below which taxes would not be paid, and all those above that level would pay their taxes. This would be done on a progressive scale. In many cases, I do not see any benefit in us giving the rich this $6'A billion. They have not invested in this country. In talking to people in other countries, one finds out
Income Tax
something that all of us should know but which I did not realize. I was talking to a person about the province of Quebec, and we were saying it would go it alone. That person said that rather than going it alone, it would become a state of the United States because the United States already owns the province: 70 per cent of the capital of Quebec comes from the United States, and if it is going anywhere, that is where it would go.
Why is the U.S. putting that kind of money into one of our provinces, or perhaps into all our provinces? They are doing so because those people to whom we allow these huge tax exemptions are not investing in Canada. They own insurance, they own stocks and bonds, but in many cases they own them in countries other than Canada.
The minister has been interested in discussing with us equality in our tax structure and how it applies. He pointed out one section in the pamphlet which indicates how the system works. For instance, in child-care they use the example of a tax credit in lieu of an income tax arrangement. A tax credit of $350 is mentioned in the pamphlet, and two women would be eligible for the same $350 credit. For the woman earning $6,000 this would mean a reduction of $93 in her tax bill. Instead of a tax saving of $257, her taxes will be reduced by $93. The woman making $20,000 would have her tax bill increased by $30. Since the present tax deduction gives her a saving of $380, but the credit only allows $350, she has to pay $30 more.
Probably everybody agrees that we should be providing free child-care in this country and we should establish free daycare centres. But we can only provide them if we obtain money from taxes to make that possible. Is there any reason why one woman with a child should be allowed greater compensation in child care allowance than another woman with a child, the only difference between them being the amount of income they earn? Is there any equality in that? These children need to be looked after in the same way. But we are giving one woman a greater allowance by giving her a tax deduction. I am sure most hon. members would say that the woman who was earning $20,000 wants her child to be better looked after. She will have to pay more for a nanny. There is a section here which discusses nannies. I understand that the Minister of Transport charged the nanny he hired half the cost of the aeroplane fare. We should look at his deductions to see if he charged a full deduction for that.

Mr. Chairman, I speak to the minister in support of the registered retirement savings plan and in support of the raising of the maximum amount from $2,500 to $3,500. I have already mentioned this in the budget debate, and I repeat it today. The reason I support the principle of RRSP is very simple. One of the ways to make our system work is to make it possible for our people to set aside some of their current earnings for their

December 20, 1976
Income Tax
future. The RRSP is far from a perfect technique, but under the present system it is a good form of saving. When this type of plan came in during the war, the principle was that if you paid into your RRSP you would defer your income tax on the amount you contributed to the plan as an inducement. That inducement, provided over the last 30 odd years, has resulted in close to 20 per cent of our Canadian wage earners participating in this form of individual saving for their future. The type of inducement the Department of Finance can provide to the Canadian people, as individuals, to look after their own individual futures has to be marked out as a success.
I do not intend in my remarks today to lay down what I think is a better system. I am speaking primarily to the minister in the hope that when he brings in his next budget he will improve on what he tried to do in his last budget in so far as registered retirement savings plans are concerned. I said that I approved the raising of the maximum from $2,500 to $3,500, for a very good reason. I do not accept the position of the NDP that his only helps rich people. This type of program is already subscribed to by approximately 20 percent of the working people of our country. In this group of working people I include not just the man who works for wages on an hourly, weekly or monthly basis; I also include the self-employed farmers of this country. I know something of the variability of income of people who are self-employed in the farming business. For years and years they went along with a net income of $2,000 per year or thereabouts, and with that amount of net income they were not able to participate too widely in plans such as this.
However, in the last three or four years, particularly in 1974 and 1975, farmers realized net income went up very dramatically in every province except Ontario, and farmers were faced with a peculiar problem which RRSPs allowed them to handle. The income of the farmer is generally very low when compared to that of the working man in the city or to that of the small businessman. When a farmer does get two or three good years and earns money beyond his immediate needs, he is able to put it into a form which will be useful to him on his retirement. Many thousands of self-employed people, particularly in the agricultural sector, have used this plan in the last two or three years.
I will now go on and discuss what the obvious next step should be, but I want to make it very clear that the opportunity for self-employed people to put aside up to $5,500 is good for this country. It is good for the individual in that he is setting some money aside with the knowledge that he saves income tax in the current year but that down the road when he wants it and does not have any more income from his selfemployment he can draw it back and pay income tax on it then.
My requests to the minister is the same request other hon. members have made. For ten years I have known, as an individual, that the weakness in the registered retirement savings plan comes about when the money is taken out. Under
(Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).)
the act it has to be taken out in the form of an annuity, and this seems fine until it is found out what these annuities yield. I know from personal experience. I got the shock of my life, when I tried to turn an RRSP into an annuity, when I realized all the sacrifice I had made to put my $700 or $800 per year into this plan, and then realized what I was going to get out of it. I could not live on that amount.
My interest has been personal, and from talking to many hundreds of people who have retired in the last six or eight years and who suddenly were caught up with inflation, I found out that the amount of money they had hoped to live on comfortably to the end of their lives-$5,000, $6,000 or $7,000 per year-turned out to be inadequate in view of the inflation of the last three or four years.
There is nothing more touching to a member of parliament than to get letters from people who have done all we have asked them to do, who have worked hard all their lives, saved their money and put it away with the expectation that the amount they would have as a result of their own effort, plus the things which are available universally, would give them a moderate standard of living until they died. This observation applies particularly to the working man. Most working men want to achieve in their lifetime a job well done, to own their home, to raise their children and to save an amount of money which, on top of the pension from their company, will be sufficient so they can live what they think is a reasonable, comfortable life without worry in the last 10, 20 or 30 years.
For these reasons the question is obvious. Since it is not really possible at this stage in this bill to get the minister to move amendments-because I know the time it would take-I ask the minister and the experts in his department to give serious consideration to preparing two or three alternative plans which could be put into the act to deal with the payment when a person wants to take out his registered retirement savings for legitimate retirement purposes.
Several alternatives have been suggested, and I am going to list two or three of them. The first one is the simplest. Since the inducement was given to the individual to put money aside in his big earning years to look after his personal needs in his retirement years-and only then would the government tax him on the money received as income-I think that principle should be held to, but held to in a way which gives the individual some choice. The first choice is obvious, to set up a special fund, which can be done at any bank, any credit union or any financial institution in Canada which allows the holding of this money, and every time the individual takes money out of that account, whether it be every month, every year or whatever, a form could be sent to the Department of National Revenue, and this should be counted as income.
There would be no bookkeeping required on the part of the Department Finance. There would be no extra administration required. This would be a simple device, and believe me, the banks and credit unions would like the business. This individual account would leave the individual maximum freedom to draw down his money as he sees fit, and if he does not need it in the first two or three years, he would not draw it down. The
December 20, 1976

interest would accumulate, and he would be asked to pay tax only when he received the income. It would be his money. The question of what happens when the man or woman dies has to arise, and the answer is very simple: it goes into the estate, and the estate is taxed.
